beginner.headline: Social Media and Concert Surprises
beginner.brief: Social media can sometimes spoil big concert surprises for fans. Many people see special moments from concerts online before they go. They might already know the songs and how the stage looks. Some fans try to avoid these spoilers to keep the excitement. Aurélia Collins tries not to see videos about her favorite artists. But other fans like to know everything before they attend a show. Some artists change their shows a little each night for new surprises.

intermediate.headline: Social Media and Live Shows: Are Spoilers Ruining the Experience?
intermediate.brief: Important performances by famous musicians are often shared quickly on social media before many fans get to see them live. Long before attending a show, fans might already know about key moments planned by their favorite artists. However, it is hard to avoid a continuous flow of videos from live shows if you use social media. Recently, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo began her Unraveled tour, and key moments from her show were quickly discussed widely online. While some fans enjoy seeing what is coming, others go to great lengths to keep the element of surprise. For example, Aurélia Collins tries to stop her social media feed from showing content about her favorite musicians. Not all fans dislike spoilers; Georgia McAdam, for instance, actually enjoys them. In response, some artists change small parts of their shows each night to create new surprises for later audiences. Music editor Laura Snapes notes that artists also benefit from these changes. Phoebe Bridgers has even banned phones from her shows to ensure fans experience true surprise.

advanced.headline: Concert Spoilers: Ruining Surprises or Building Excitement?
advanced.brief: Social media is significantly altering the concert experience, with "big moments from headline acts" often shared online long before many fans attend the actual shows. Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned. You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view. For many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos if you're online, whether you like it or not. For instance, surprises from Olivia Rodrigo's Unraveled tour, which scores of fans paid a lot for, have already been "dissected online". While some fans "lap up" the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking "extreme measures" to preserve the element of surprise. Aurélia Collins, a dedicated fan, spends weeks trying to "trick her algorithm" into not serving her content about favourite artists. She finds this effort "worth it for the surprise," even if it means her social media feed is a bit bland. Collins was "gutted" when a spoiler about Niall Horan slipped through, just before her first live show after 16 years of fandom. She explains that because she couldn't afford live music when younger, she now really wants to "take it in" such a moment. She wants the "full experience," emphasizing the element of surprise that people attending the opening night can get. Not all fans view spoilers negatively; Georgia McAdam claims she loves them. McAdam sees online spoilers more as "teasers" and believes no amount of videos can diminish the excitement of the real thing. She acknowledges that sometimes artists offer different "surprise songs" or unexpected actions at shows. Some artists react by "switching up" their sets in small ways each night to ensure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected. For example, Taylor Swift featured "bespoke outfits" and surprise songs, while Sabrina Carpenter and Jay-Z also varied their shows. Laura Snapes, deputy music editor for The Guardian, notes that artists can ensure "they're staying in the press" by having something different happen nightly. Snapes adds that if fans want to be surprised, they "have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture" by avoiding online content. Phoebe Bridgers is taking things further by banning phones altogether at her shows. Attendees must lock their phones and recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out. McAdam would not support a ban on phones, arguing that recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for many fans. Conversely, Collins states she is "not totally against it" regarding phone bans. What Collins would prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos to give fans the option for surprise. Ultimately, Snapes suggests that even with set list knowledge, fans may still witness "moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned." She cites Taylor Swift blowing her nose during the Edinburgh Eras show as an example of an unscripted moment.
